chapter_theme: Songs at Palani (பழநி, 5 of 7): the poet confesses lust and courtesans who take a man's property, his faults and sins, disease and Death's rope, and the vain praise of patrons and court poets, and asks for Murugan's feet, service and knowledge; the praise turns on Murugan as Siva's child guru who spoke the pranava, the race for the fruit that brought him to Palani, the Tamil saint who cured the Pandya, and Vishnu as uncle.
structure_note: Courtesan and love songs (169, 172, 177, 178, and 164, a love-lament in another voice); lists of self-accusation (167, 174) and of diseases (166); Death and rebirth (165, 168); two songs against patrons and court poets (171, 175); the litany 170; and 176, a song of praise alone that tells the Palani story of the fruit.

164.reading: A love-lament, apparently in a mother's or companion's voice: through Kama's bow, the dark roaring sea with its rolling pearls and the evening when the light fades, the creeper-like girl has lost speech and sense and her life grows faint, and Murugan is asked to give her his garland. The praise names him the hero who imprisoned the lotus-born Brahma, the one who melted for Devayanai, and the one who told a word to Siva of the radiant matted hair, at Palani.
164.nuance: The speaker never says 'I': the girl is கொடி, the creeper, and the plea is for Murugan's garland (நற்பிணையல்) for her, the stock request of akam poems addressed to a god. The metre and machinery (Kama's arrows, the sea, the evening) match 24. The first lines split uncertainly.

165.reading: The poet asks that before fierce-eyed Death throws his twisted rope around his head, when kin, friends, house, wealth and power become strangers, Murugan grant him thought of his two feet, end his loneliness and give him knowledge. The praise names Kumara of war, the lord of Palani hill, the hunter girl's bridegroom, the destroyer of the asuras who troubled the gods, the owner of dharma, colour, the peacock and the vel.
165.nuance: அயலாக, become strangers, is the point: at Death's coming everything owned turns foreign, and the poet names his state தனிமை, loneliness. மயிலும் அயிலும் is a play on peacock and vel.

166.reading: The poet lists the diseases (headache, jaundice, anaemia, fever, eye pain, colic, asthma) and asks that they not come near, nor the indignity of physicians who name remedies, turn deaf, and demand payment for failing age; and asks that, like the sages who gather flowers for garlands to adorn his feet and hold them in their hearts, he may be given the feet, with Murugan coming on the peacock that lifts the snake. The praise names Rama who bridged the sea, cut Ravana's crowns and brought back Janaki, as uncle; Siva who danced in the hall to shame Kali, to whom Murugan came as a father; and the hunter girl on her platform, at Palani.
166.nuance: The list of illnesses (தலைவலி, காமாலை, சோகை, சுரம், சூலை, காயாசுவாசம்) is unusually medical. The physicians' lines are hard to parse: who turns deaf and who is asked to give (தாரீர்) is not certain. மாதாதையே எனவும் வருவோனே again makes Murugan father to his father, the teacher's rank.

167.reading: A short song of self-accusation: the poet says he has no firmness, no good quality, no skill, no wonderful deed, no true penance, no japa, no place in heaven, no giving hand and no fit speech, and asks that he may sing good Tamil, reach the two feet, be rid of both kinds of deeds and gain the destined state. The praise names the vel against the asuras and Murugan as son of the dancer whose matted hair wears the crescent, arugu, konrai and crane feather, at Palani.
167.nuance: The confession is built of negatives in -இலி (திடமிலி, சற்குணமிலி, தவமிலி, கொடையிலி); the remedy is first to sing Tamil (நற்றமிழ் பாட) and then to be rid of இருவினை, good and bad deeds alike.

168.reading: The poet asks that if Murugan leaves him in birth, which is like a dark sea of hell, he not be deaf, blind, deformed or the least poor, but have a fine form, high family, knowledge and fullness, and that Murugan give his grace and come to take him, mind and all, into service. The praise names the vel that made the asuras' heads roll, the sea wail and the mountain break, Vishnu on the serpent bed as uncle and the dark-throated Siva as father, at Palani.
168.nuance: The plea is conditional and practical: if rebirth must come (விடுவாயேல்), let it be a whole and fortunate one, then service. It does not ask for release outright.

169.reading: The poet quotes his own wooing of women (peacock, lotus, deer, honey who knows every art of love, come to my breasts, give me your lips, I swear I will be your slave) and says he wandered so, a great sinner without justice, infatuated, and never chanted Murugan's name, joined his devotees or wore ash; yet he asks for the anklets so that the servant may be saved. The praise tells the churning of the ocean, Siva taking the poison and Vishnu as the enchantress sharing the nectar, as uncle, and the generous lord of Kalisai on the Kaveri, at Veerai and Palani.
169.nuance: Unusually the poet's own pleading speech to women is quoted (என் ஆணை மொழி சோர்வதிலை, யான் அடிமையாவேன்): he offers them the servitude (அடிமை) he owes Murugan, and the song turns on that word. The omissions are worship's marks: chanting, devotees, ash on the forehead (நீறு நுதல்மீதிடலிலன்). The patron of Kalisai is praised as a cloud in giving.

170.reading: A litany of homage (நமோநம): Murugan beyond nada, bindu and kala, the form of Vedic mantra, the scholar of knowledge, son of Sambhu, lord of the serpent-bound peacock, the one who split the Suras, the lamp of auspicious light, Devayanai's lord; the poet asks never to forget giving, worship with many rites, recitation, good conduct, kindness and service at the guru's feet. The praise names him lord of Vayalur in the Chola land of the Kaveri and recalls the Chera king who rode with Sundarar to Kailas and sang the Ula, at Avinankudi in the Kongu land.
170.nuance: நாத விந்து கலாதீ puts Murugan beyond the tattvas of Saiva cosmology. The plea is a short list of practice (ஈதல், பூஜை, ஓதல், குருசீர்பாத சேவை), not a confession. The last lines recall Cheraman Perumal's ride to Kailas with Sundarar (ஆரூரர் தோழமை, the horse, the Ula).

171.reading: The poet attacks court poets who learn petty verses, call them Veda, boast daily, win titles, palanquins, umbrellas, rings and earrings, but whose learning breaks and changes colour when tested, and asks that he may stand before Murugan and speak fine words with full devotion. The praise tells how a pinch of ash from a small hand cured the Pandya of the fever the Jains had set on him and the Jains were impaled, and how Murugan took as his hereditary servant a fool who embraced women without limit and a sinner dazed by impurity, at Palani.
171.nuance: The target is professional learning: titles and regalia (சத்ர சாமர, மோதிரம், குண்டலம்) without substance. The cure of செழியன் with ash from a child's hand (சிறிய கர பங்கயத்து நீறு) is Sambandar's story, credited to Murugan as in 149 and 150. The poet calls himself the one taken into வழியடிமை, inherited service. Some lines of the confession are unclear.

172.reading: The poet describes kohl-eyed women who stand in the street with sweating foreheads and swaying breasts, delude men daily on flower beds, take every possession under friendship and invent new tricks each day, and asks that, instead of their company, Murugan give him a cool mind of true devotion. The praise names Siva who gave paddy to a learned Tamil poet, Devayanai whom the elephant of heaven raised, Vishnu with the conch as uncle, and Palani where the drummers' mridangam sounds like thunder.
172.nuance: மெத்தவும் நட்பொடு பறித்து, robbing under friendship, is the courtesan charge. மெய்ப்படு பத்தி, true devotion, and உட்குளிர் புத்தி, a cool mind, are what is asked. The story of Siva giving paddy to a poet (நெல் பல அளித்த) I cannot identify with certainty.

173.reading: The poet confesses that he has not learned a few songs of fine Tamil in music or known the epics, and that through women with coral lips he wanders the sea-girt earth like a dry leaf; before his body thins he asks Murugan to come on the dancing peacock. The praise names him as the child who drank the milk Uma poured, Vishnu who came in a moment to save the elephant from the crocodile as uncle, and the guru who told Hara the meaning of the first letter, at Thiruvavinankudi in Palani.
173.nuance: The confession sets neglected Tamil learning beside lust. உமை மொழியிற் பொழி பாலை உண்டிடு பாலன் is Sambandar, fed by Uma, again identified with Murugan. அகரப் பொருள் ஆதி ஒன்றிடு முதல் அக்கரம் is the meaning of the first syllable, the pranava, told to Siva.

174.reading: The poet lists his sins: guilty of the five great crimes, a total fool, deceitful, a miser, a gambler, a killer, seeking women, house and gold, held by the five malas and bonds and by the five elements, who never joined the devotees of grace; and asks to be granted to play in Kanda's world, where the consort of the moon-crowned Siva, the light Vishnu and Brahma could not find, plays. The praise names the vel against Sura's army, the sea and Krauncha, Murugan as son of Uma, Rama's sister, called Sivakami, Kali and Mangala, and the hunter girl, at Palani.
174.nuance: பஞ்ச பாதகன் (guilty of the five great sins) and பஞ்ச மாமலம் (five impurities) set the confession in Siddhanta terms. The goal named is கந்த நாடு, Kanda's world, a heaven rather than union. Uma as Rama's sister (ரகுராமர் இட தங்கை) follows the tradition that makes Vishnu Uma's brother.

175.reading: The poet describes singing great poems to patrons, praising them as Pari in giving, a cloud, mighty-shouldered, famed in seven worlds, the light of the world and Indra's equal, only to be met with anger and no pity and to wilt at their doors in vain, while others carry off the poem and waste it; he asks whether those who do not think of Murugan can come near him. The praise names Vishnu, who saved the elephant crying 'first cause' from the crocodile, as uncle, Murugan with twelve hands on the peacock, and the servant from Kalisai, at Veerai and Palani.
175.nuance: The patrons are flattered with the stock comparisons (பாரியான கொடை, கொண்டலே), the very praise the poet now regrets (சீறுவார் கடையிற் சென்று). The closing question turns the complaint: men who do not think of Murugan are unworthy of praise. Vishnu saving the elephant (மூலமென் ஆரவாரம்) parallels 173.

176.reading: A song of praise alone: Siva, who burned the cities with a smile, is made clear in mind when the child guru speaks the secret of the pranava into his golden ear; Murugan fights the asuras until the mountains turn to dust and blood overflows the sea. When Siva gave the fruit to the elephant-faced one for circling his feet while Murugan circled the world, Murugan grew angry that it was not given to him and came to dwell at Palani, Sivagiri.
176.nuance: This is the Palani legend: பொற்கிரியைத் தனி வலம் வர (circling the golden mountain, the world), அக்கனியைத் தரவிலை என வெகுண்டு (angry that the fruit was not given). The anger is told plainly and the shrine is its result. பொற்செவியுட் பிரணவ ரகசியம் ... உரைசெய் குழந்தைக் குருநாதா names the pranava. One line is corrupt.

177.reading: The poet confesses that, embracing women's adorned breasts daily, he has become helpless, chaff in understanding, a worthless fool, and asks Murugan, with incomparable grace, to speak one word to his servant. The praise names him the younger brother of the elephant with temples like pots and the vel that rushed on the asura army, at Palani with its dripping banana clusters and sugarcane fields.
177.nuance: அறிவிற் பதடி, chaff in understanding, and அசடன் are the self-names. The plea for 'one word' (ஒருசொல் புகல்வாயே) echoes the word Murugan spoke to Siva, asked now for the poet.

178.reading: The poet describes women with breasts like tusks, crescent brows, vel eyes and night-dark hair, who question those who come with property at their houses and carry it away, deceitful at heart, and says that, infatuated, he melted, wasted and whirled in deeds; he asks for the bliss of knowledge to worship Murugan's feet. The praise names the vel that restored the gods, Murugan circling the earth on the peacock in a moment with devotees crying 'Hara', and Krishna who was tied with a rope and ate curd from the hanging pot, at Palani by the great river.
178.nuance: உரியதோர் பொருள்கொடு வந்த பேர்களை மனையிலே வினவியே கொண்டுபோகிய: the women take the property men bring, and the verse calls them வஞ்ச மாதர்கள். The poet's state is மயல், and the result is bodily wasting (உடலற வெம்பி).

links.note: Both are love-laments in the same short metre over a lovesick girl, worn down by Kama's arrows, the sea or south wind, and evening; both name Murugan as the one who spoke a word to Siva. 24 is plainly the mother's voice; 164 asks Murugan for his garland for the girl.

Both confess the poet's trade of praising patrons for gifts. 15 regrets it with a wounded heart and asks for service instead; 175 adds the patrons' contempt and asks whether men who do not think of Murugan deserve to be sung at all.
Both credit Murugan with Sambandar's victory over the Jains, who are impaled, and with the holy ash: in 149 the ash is spread through the town, in 171 a pinch of it cures the Pandya king.
153 alludes to the race round the world in one line; 176 tells the whole story, including Murugan's anger at losing the fruit, and makes it the reason he dwells at Palani.
The Kural warns of women who weigh the profit and then speak of their goodness; 172 describes the same pretence from inside, women who take every possession 'with great friendship'.
Both make a man's welcome depend on what he brings: the Naladiyar's courtesans find a moneyed oil-presser sugar, and 178's women question at the door those who come with property and carry it off.

The Kural's woman says that with her lover away the evening comes like enemies to a killing ground (கொலைக்களத்து ஏதிலர் போல வரும்). 164 lines up Kama's bow, the roaring sea and the hour when the light fades (ஒளிமட்கு மிகைப் பொழுதாலே) as attackers through which the creeper-girl's life grows faint (உயிர் எய்த்த). The song carries the Kural's hostile evening into a plea to the god for his garland.

165 asks that when kin, house, wealth and power become strangers (அயலாக) before Death's rope, Murugan's feet end his loneliness (எனது தனிமை கழிய). The Tirumanthiram names the Lord as the one whom those without kin take as kin (சுற்றற்றவர் சுற்றுக் கருதிய). The song asks for exactly the kinship the Tirumanthiram says the Lord gives the kinless.

The Tirumanthiram's kin rise wailing but turn back at the edge of the town (ஊர்த்துறைக் காலே ஒழிவர்) and then light the pyre. 165 says that at Death's coming kin, friends and house all turn into strangers (தமரும் அமரும் மனையும் ... அயலாக). Both see the bonds of kin end at death; the song draws from it a plea for the feet.

The Tirumanthiram's dying man is let go by the physician after the pulse is felt (கைவிட்டு நாடி) while wife and wealth stay behind. 166 asks to be spared both the diseases and physicians who name remedies, turn deaf and ask payment for failing age (சரியும் வயதுக்கு ஏது தாரீர்). Both make the physician the figure who fails at the end.

The Tirumanthiram says the great medicine (மாமருந்து), like mantra and the pure path, is the Lord's pair of feet. 166 lists headache, jaundice, fever and colic and the physicians' useless cures, and asks instead for the two feet that sages hold in their hearts (இருபாதம் உளமது தரித்தே). The song applies the Tirumanthiram's claim to a catalogue of real illness.

Tirumular asks why people seek a later birth when they do no tapas beforehand, and says the Lord made him to render the Lord well in Tamil (தன்னை நன்றாகத் தமிழ் செய்யுமாறே). 167 confesses he has no tapas or japa (தவமிலி, செபமிலி) and asks first that he may sing good Tamil (நற்றமிழ் பாட), then reach the feet and be rid of both deeds. The song takes the Tirumanthiram's way out, Tamil in place of the missing tapas, as its own plea.

Both songs build the poet's self-portrait from privative names: 167 with -இலி (திடமிலி, தவமிலி, கொடையிலி), 320 with -இலன் (தவமிலன், புகலிலன், பொறையிலன், கலையிலன்). 167 asks to sing Tamil; 320 lacks the art of learning Murugan's praise. The same device in distant chapters makes the lack of song itself part of the confession.

The Tirumanthiram says that one born of two who sought pleasure and grown in painful bondage can still, once born, seek the Ancient and chant (தொன்புற நாடிநின்று ஓதலுமாமே). 168 accepts that Murugan may leave him in birth (செனனம் அதனில் விடுவாயேல்) and asks only for a whole body, family and knowledge, and to be taken into service. Both treat birth not as the end of hope but as a place from which service is still possible.

Tirumular took on servitude to the servants of the Lord's servants and the Lord took him, saying this one is my servant (அடியான் இவன் என்று அடிமைகொண்டானே). 169 quotes his oath to women, I will be your slave (யான் அடிமையாவேன்), confesses he never joined the Lord's devotees (அடியாரோடு கூடுகிலன்), and asks that this servant be redeemed (யானடிமை ஈடேறவே). The pairing shows the same அடிமை offered to the wrong master and the right one.

The Kural says an unlearned man's standing wilts once he meets others and speaks (சொல்லாடச் சோர்வு படும்). 171 says the court poets' learning, decked with titles and regalia, breaks and changes colour when tested (முடிவில் அவை ஒன்றும் அற்று வேறொரு நிறமாகி முறியும்). Both make the test of speech the place where false learning collapses.

The Naladiyar's worthless woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from men's hands (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு) and then balks. 172's women take every possession under the guise of friendship (பொருட்கள் யாவையும் மெத்தவும் நட்பொடு பறித்து) and invent new tricks daily. Both locate the fraud in affection used as the instrument of taking.

The Tirumanthiram says even one guilty of the five great sins (அதிபஞ்ச பாதகன்) escapes hell if he gives to the Lord, the guru and those free of desire and learns from them. 174 calls himself guilty of the five great sins (பஞ்ச பாதகன்) and also a miser (லோபியன்) headed for hell, who never joined the devotees. The Tirumanthiram names the condition of rescue, giving, and 174 confesses lacking exactly that.

The Kural calls the man who parades useless words not a man but chaff among men (மக்கட் பதடி). 177 names himself chaff in understanding (அறிவிற் பதடி), a fool made helpless by daily embraces, and asks for one word of grace. The rare word பதடி carries the Kural's contempt into the poet's self-judgement.

source_issues: Song 166: one corrupt character in தா஡ணர் (line 6); probably தாரீர் ('give').
Song 169: one corrupt character in தா஡ணரெ (line 5); probably தாரீரே ('give').
Song 170: one corrupt character in வயலு஡ரா (line 18); clearly வயலூரா. Also the unflagged garble அர்ருரர் (line 19), probably ஆரூரர் (Sundarar).
Song 171: the unflagged garble மல்ருபம் (line 21); a letter seems lost, perhaps மலரூபம்.
Song 174: one corrupt character in கடலு஡டு (line 3); clearly கடலூடு.
Song 176: one corrupt character in தன஧முவ (line 6); the word cannot be restored with confidence.
